title: The Languages of Middle-earth
blurb: Middle-earth has many languages: two Elvish tongues, the secret speech of Dwarves, the Common Speech of Men, and the Black Speech of Mordor.
book:
The Elves spoke two main tongues in the Third Age. Quenya was the ancient High-elven speech of Valinor. Sindarin was the Grey-elven speech of Beleriand and the common Elvish language of Middle-earth in later ages.

The Dwarves kept their own tongue, Khuzdul, private. They used other languages with outsiders. Men spoke many tongues. The most widespread was Westron, also called the Common Speech. It grew from the language of Númenor and served Men, Hobbits and many others in the west.

Sauron made the Black Speech for his servants. He failed in that aim. Orcs had no tongue of their own. They took words from other languages, many from the Black Speech. Their dialects differed so much that they often used the Common Speech between tribes.

The Ents had a slow, rich language of their own. The Rohirrim spoke Rohirric, and the Dunlendings and Drúedain had other tongues. Tolkien presents the Red Book as a translation. English stands in for Westron, and Old English stands in for Rohirric.

Writing also differed. Elves used the Tengwar, and Dwarves and some others used the Cirth, the runes.

The books say little of the languages of the far East and South. Tolkien left many of them unnamed.

places.note: The Rohirrim speak a tongue related to the languages of the Northmen.
Rivendell is a house of Elvish lore and speech.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix E
The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion

title: Quenya
blurb: Quenya is the ancient High-elven language of Valinor, used in the Third Age mainly for lore, ceremony, formal names and song.
book:
Quenya was the speech of the Noldor and the Vanyar in Valinor. The Noldor carried it back to Middle-earth when they left the Blessed Realm.

In Beleriand it met trouble. After the Kinslaying at Alqualondë, Thingol forbade its use in his lands. The Noldor then took up Sindarin for daily speech. Quenya survived among them as a language of lore.

By the Third Age Quenya was no longer a mother tongue in Middle-earth. Elves still sang in it and used it in formal speech. The Dúnedain also kept it. Many Númenórean royal names were Quenya, and Gondor's kings took Quenya throne-names. Aragorn's name Elessar is Quenya.

Galadriel's lament in Lothlórien, Namárië, is in Quenya. Quenya words also appear in the Oath of Elendil, which Aragorn used when he took the crown.

Appendix F calls it a kind of Elven-latin. It was no longer a mother tongue, but it was kept for ceremony, lore and song.

It is written most often in the Tengwar.

places.note: Galadriel sings her farewell lament in Quenya here.
Elrond's house keeps Elvish lore in both High-elven and Grey-elven.

sources: The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapter 15
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 8
The Return of the King, Book VI, chapter 5

title: Sindarin
blurb: Sindarin is the Grey-elven language of Beleriand and the everyday Elvish speech of Middle-earth in the Third Age.
book:
Sindarin grew from the speech of the Elves who stayed in Middle-earth while others went west. In Beleriand it changed a great deal over the long years of the First Age.

The Noldor learned it quickly after their return. After Thingol banned Quenya, the exiles used Sindarin as their daily language. Later it spread among Elves of Eriador, Lindon and Rivendell.

Many names in the books come from it. Imladris, Lothlórien, Mithrandir and Mordor are Sindarin names. Most place-names of Gondor are Sindarin, because the Dúnedain valued Elvish speech. Few Men used it daily.

Silvan Elves spoke their own older tongues but used Sindarin when talking with the Eldar, with an accent. Legolas and Haldir speak it naturally.

The book shows Sindarin on the West-gate of Moria. The inscription invites a friend to speak and enter. Gandalf at last sees that the password is simply the Sindarin word for friend.

Sindarin appears in both Tengwar and Cirth, depending on who writes it.

places.note: The Sindarin inscription and password are on the Doors of Durin.
Elves of Eriador use Sindarin daily here.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 4
The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapters 13 and 15

title: Khuzdul
blurb: Khuzdul is the language of the Dwarves, kept secret from outsiders. Only a few of its words are known in the books.
book:
The Dwarves say that Aulë, their maker, devised their language before they woke. They treasured it and taught it to no one outside their folk. Dwarves in Middle-earth used other languages with other peoples.

For this reason the books record very little Khuzdul. Dwarves give outsiders names taken from the speech of Men, usually Northern names. Thorin, Dwalin and Gimli are such outer names. The true names of Dwarves are secret and are never revealed to others.

A few words survive. Khazad means Dwarves, and the old city of Khazad-dûm takes its name from it. Gimli cries a war-shout in Khuzdul at the Hornburg. The Elvish name Belegost for a Dwarf-city of the west stands beside its Dwarvish name, Gabilgathol.

Other Dwarvish place-names are given in the languages of those who named them, such as Moria, Dwarrowdelf and Hadhodrond. Even the Elves knew little of the language.

When Dwarves wrote, they used runes, the Cirth, for Khuzdul as well as for the Common Speech. Tombs and records show this.

places.note: Gimli shouts his war-cry in Khuzdul during the defence of the Hornburg.
The Dwarvish name Khazad-dûm belongs to this realm.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (Durin's Folk)
The Two Towers, Book III, chapter 7
The Silmarillion, chapter 10

title: Westron (the Common Speech)
blurb: Westron, the Common Speech, was the main language of Men in the west and was used by Hobbits, Dwarves and others for trade and daily talk.
book:
Westron grew from Adûnaic, the language of Númenor. In the Second Age it was spoken in the Númenórean forts and havens on the coasts of Middle-earth. There it mixed with the tongues of Men and spread. Over the centuries it became the language that most peoples of the west could understand.

Gondor and Arnor spoke it as a native tongue. By the time of the War of the Ring even many Elves understood it. Hobbits spoke a form of it with local words, and Dwarves and Orcs used it with outsiders.

The Dúnedain of Gondor kept Elvish names for places and persons. They also took many Elvish words into Westron. That gave the Common Speech a mix of Númenórean and Elvish sounds.

Tolkien presents the Red Book as a translation from Westron. English stands for it. Tolkien tells us that many names are also translated. Hobbit family names and place names such as Bag End are translations of Westron names. Tolkien says the same of the names of Hobbit months and days.

The Rohirrim spoke their own language and used Westron with the Gondorians.

facts.Root: Adûnaic, spoken in the Númenórean havens

places.note: Westron became the native tongue of the Men of Gondor.
Hobbits spoke Westron with local words and humour.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F, 'Of Men'
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F, 'On Translation'

title: The Black Speech
blurb: The Black Speech is the language that Sauron devised for his servants. Only a few words appear in the books.
book:
Sauron made the Black Speech in the Dark Years of the Second Age. He wanted all his servants to share one tongue.

He failed in that aim. Many words of the Black Speech spread among the Orcs, but they twisted them into many dialects. Orcs of different tribes often fell back on the Common Speech to talk with each other.

After his first downfall, the ancient form of the Black Speech was forgotten by all but the Nazgûl. Sauron revived it in the Third Age when he rose again in Mordor.

The best-known example is the verse on the One Ring. It is written in the Elvish script. Gandalf speaks it aloud at the Council of Elrond. His voice turns harsh, a shadow seems to pass over the sun, and the Elves stop their ears. Afterwards Elrond rebukes him, for no one had ever spoken that tongue in Rivendell.

The books give a few other words. The words Nazgûl and Uruk come from it. Orc names such as Grishnákh and Uglúk have the same harsh sound.

Tolkien never tells us everything about the Black Speech.

places.note: Barad-dûr is the seat of the lord who made this tongue.
Gandalf speaks the Ring verse at the Council of Elrond here.

sources: The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 2
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Two Towers, Book III, chapter 3

title: The Tongue of Rohan and Other Languages of Men
blurb: The Rohirrim spoke Rohirric, a tongue like the speech of the Northmen. Other Men had Dunlending, Drúedain and Southron languages.
book:
The Rohirrim spoke Rohirric. It was related to the languages of the Northmen of the Anduin vales, from whom they came. They used the Common Speech with the Men of Gondor, though they kept their own speech in the Mark.

Tolkien makes Rohirric look like Old English, and he treats the Rohirrim names as English. Théoden, Éomer, Meduseld and Edoras are in this style. Théoden calls the Hobbits holbytlan, hole-builders. Appendix F treats the word hobbit as a worn-down form of a Rohirric word of this kind.

The men of Dale used names that look like Old Norse. Bard and Brand are examples. Beorn belongs to the same group of northern Men.

The Dunlendings spoke their own tongue and hated the Rohirrim. The Drúedain, the Wild Men of the Drúadan Forest, had their own speech. Ghân-buri-Ghân speaks the Common Speech only haltingly.

The Men of Harad and the Easterlings used other languages. Tolkien does not name them, and he gives almost nothing of their words.

places.note: Edoras and Meduseld carry Rohirric names rendered in an Old English style.
The Dunlendings kept their own tongue.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Two Towers, Book III, chapter 8
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (The House of Eorl)
The Return of the King, Book V, chapter 5

title: The Tengwar
blurb: The Tengwar is the flowing Elvish script that Fëanor designed. It is used for many languages and appears on the Ring and the Doors of Durin.
book:
The Tengwar were devised by Fëanor in Valinor. He built on the older letters of Rúmil of Tirion, which were never used in Middle-earth. The exiled Noldor brought the Fëanorian letters to Middle-earth.

The script is systematic. Letters are formed from a stem and a bow, and families of related letters form series. The shape of a letter shows its place in the sound system. This is not an alphabet in the Latin sense. It is a scheme designed by a loremaster.

In many modes, vowels are marked by small signs placed above the consonants. Writers can adapt the same letters to different languages, which are called modes. Elvish, Westron and even the Black Speech were written in it in the Third Age.

The Ring inscription is in Tengwar. So is the writing on the West-gate of Moria. It is drawn in ithildin, which shows only under the light of the moon and the stars.

The Tengwar suited pen and brush. The Cirth were made mainly for carving, and the Dwarves often used them.

facts.Used for: Quenya, Sindarin, Westron and the Black Speech

places.note: The Doors of Durin carry an inscription in Tengwar.
The Ring inscription is read in Elrond's hall.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix E
The Silmarillion, Quenta Silmarillion, chapter 6
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapters 2 and 4

title: The Cirth (Runes)
kind: Runic script of Elves and Dwarves
blurb: The Cirth are the angular runes devised in Beleriand and later adopted by the Dwarves. They are used mainly for carving and inscriptions.
book:
The Cirth were first devised by the Sindar of Beleriand to write Sindarin. Daeron, the minstrel and loremaster of Doriath, later arranged and enlarged them. That fuller form is called the Alphabet of Daeron. It was later used and enlarged in Eregion.

The Dwarves of Moria took the runes and adapted them for their own tongue. Dwarvish loremasters rearranged the signs. These forms are called the runes of Moria, and Dwarves across Middle-earth used them.

Because the Cirth are angular, they are well suited to carving on stone, wood and metal. The Dwarves used them on tombs, in books and on maps. Balin's tomb in Moria bears a Cirth inscription.

The Book of Mazarbul is written in runes of Moria and of Dale, with Elvish letters here and there. The mixture shows that the Dwarves of the colony used both scripts. Thrór's Map shows runes too. Elrond reads its moon letters, which show only when a moon of the same shape and season shines behind them.

Elves later preferred the Tengwar.

facts.Inventor: The Sindar; enlarged by Daeron of Doriath

places.note: Balin's tomb bears an inscription in the runes of Moria.
The Book of Mazarbul was found in this chamber of Moria.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix E
The Hobbit, chapter 3
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapters 4 and 5

title: Shire Reckoning and the Shire Calendar
blurb: Hobbits counted years from the founding of the Shire. Their calendar had twelve thirty-day months and a few extra holidays.
book:
Shire Reckoning counts years from the settlement of the Shire in T.A. 1601. That year is S.R. 1. The brothers Marcho and Blanco led the Hobbits across the Brandywine with the permission of the King at Fornost. So T.A. 3018 is S.R. 1418, the year Frodo left Bag End. Bilbo's farewell party was in S.R. 1401, or T.A. 3001.

The year has twelve months of thirty days each. Their names are Afteryule, Solmath, Rethe, Astron, Thrimidge, Forelithe, Afterlithe, Wedmath, Halimath, Winterfilth, Blotmath and Foreyule.

Five extra days fall outside the months. Two Yule days mark the end of one year and the start of the next. Three Lithe days stand at midsummer. The middle one is Midyear's Day. A leap year adds the Overlithe after Midyear's Day.

The week has seven days, called Sterday, Sunday, Monday, Trewsday, Hevensday, Mersday and Highday. Highday is the last and chief day of the week. It is a holiday from noon, with feasts in the evening.

Midyear's Day and the Overlithe have no weekday. So each year begins on the same day of the week, and a given date always falls on the same weekday.

facts.Extra days: Yule, Lithe days and the Overlithe in leap years

places.note: Shire Reckoning begins with the founding of the Shire.
The King's seat at Fornost gave the Hobbits leave to settle.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix D
The Lord of the Rings, Prologue, 'Concerning Hobbits'

title: The Calendars of the Elves, the Kings and the Stewards
blurb: Appendix D describes three older calendars: the Elvish one, the Reckoning of the Kings used in Númenor and Arnor, and the Stewards' Reckoning of Gondor.
book:
The Elves counted time in long spans. A yén was a period of 144 solar years. Their solar year, the loa, had six seasons: tuilë, lairë, yávië, quellë, hrívë and coirë. The Elvish week, the enquië, had six days.

The Númenóreans used the Reckoning of the Kings. It was kept in Númenor and later in Arnor and Gondor. It has a seven-day week and twelve months with Quenya names, such as Narvinyë, Nénimë and Súlimë. Ten months had thirty days and two had thirty-one. Three more days stood outside the months: one at the start of the year, one at midsummer and one at the end. That makes 365 days. In a leap year the midsummer day was doubled.

In Gondor the Stewards later adopted a revised calendar, the Stewards' Reckoning. In it every month had thirty days. Two new days outside the months were added, one in spring and one in autumn. Mardil, the first Ruling Steward, is linked with the change. Most users of the Common Speech adopted it, but the Hobbits did not.

After the fall of Sauron, the restored kingdom began the New Reckoning. It returned to the Kings' Reckoning, but its year began in spring, on 25 March by the old count, in memory of Sauron's downfall.

The Shire kept its own calendar, which had grown out of the Kings' Reckoning.

Appendix D gives full tables for anyone who wishes to compare the systems.

places.note: Gondor used the Stewards' Reckoning from this city.
Elrond's house kept the Elvish lore of the calendar.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix D

title: Customs of Hobbits
blurb: Hobbits love gifts, good food and comfort. Their customs include birthday presents, mathoms, round homes and many meals.
book:
Hobbits give presents on their own birthdays. The host hands them out to the guests. Bilbo's eleventy-first birthday party was famous for its gifts.

A mathom is an object that has no clear use but that nobody wishes to throw away. Hobbits pass them on as gifts. The Mathom-house at Michel Delving held many that were never given away.

Hobbits like homes with round doors and windows, all on one floor, dug into banks and hillsides. Such a home is called a smial. Bag End in Hobbiton and the Great Smials of Tuckborough are examples. By the time of the story many Hobbits lived in ordinary houses.

Meals matter greatly. The Prologue says Hobbits like six meals a day when they can get them.

Hobbits also keep long family records. They are fond of pipe-weed, beer and tales of their forebears. Most prefer not to go far from home.

They laugh easily, they go barefoot, and most of them distrust adventures.
film: In the 2001 film Pippin asks about second breakfast, and Merry adds elevenses, luncheon, afternoon tea, dinner and supper.

places.note: Bag End is the best-known Hobbit smial.
The Mathom-house stores unwanted gifts and curiosities.
The Great Smials is the Took family's huge home.
The Mathom-house stands in the chief town of the Shire.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Prologue, 'Concerning Hobbits'
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapters 1 and 2
The Hobbit, chapter 1

title: The Government of the Shire
kind: Offices and officers of the Shire
blurb: The Shire has a Thain, a Mayor, the Master of Buckland, Shirriffs and Bounders. Few laws are enforced, and most Hobbits keep to old customs.
book:
The Shire has little government. Hobbits obey the old Rules, which are mostly customs from the days of the King.

The Thain held the authority of the vanished King. The office passed from the Oldbucks to the Tooks. The Thain was master of the Shire-moot and captain of the Shire-muster and the Hobbitry-in-arms. These met only in emergencies, so by Bilbo's time the office was mostly a title.

The Mayor of Michel Delving was the only real official. He was elected every seven years at the Free Fair on the White Downs at Midsummer. He presided at banquets on Shire holidays. He was also Postmaster and First Shirriff.

Buckland is part of the Shire but has its own ruler, the Master of Buckland, who is a Brandybuck.

The Shirriffs are the police. There were twelve, three in each Farthing. They dealt more with stray beasts than with people. A larger body, the Bounders, beat the bounds and kept Outsiders from making a nuisance of themselves.

In Frodo's time, Lotho's men misuse these offices. The Shirriffs become his police, and the Hobbits must rise to restore order.

facts.Mayor elected: Every seven years at the Free Fair, at Midsummer

places.note: The Mayor lives and works in Michel Delving.
Shirriff-houses serve as the Shirriffs' lodgings.
The Master of Buckland rules this land.
Brandy Hall is the seat of the Master of Buckland.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Prologue, 'Of the Ordering of the Shire'
The Return of the King, Book VI, chapter 8

title: The Three Kinds of Hobbits
blurb: Hobbits came in three kinds. Harfoots were the commonest, Stoors loved rivers and Fallohides were fair, tall and fond of Elves.
book:
Hobbits of the Third Age were descended from three groups: Harfoots, Stoors and Fallohides. They moved from the Anduin vales into Eriador in stages. Appendix B dates the Harfoots there about T.A. 1050, and the Fallohides and Stoors about T.A. 1150. By the time of the story the kinds had mixed.

Harfoots were small, brown and beardless. They went barefoot and lived in hills and holes. They were the most numerous and the first to cross the mountains.

Stoors were broader and heavier than the others. They preferred river country and boats, and they were more at ease with Men. Some wore boots in muddy lands. Gandalf guesses that Gollum's people were akin to the Stoors. They lived by the river near the Gladden Fields.

Fallohides were fairer and taller, and slimmer too. They liked woods and had friendships with Elves. They were bolder than other Hobbits and often became leaders. The Tooks and the Masters of Buckland have a strong Fallohide strain.

The Shire holds a mix of all three. Stoors lingered long in the Angle and in Dunland. Some later went back east to the Wild, and others moved west.

Appendix and Prologue give no exact count of any group.
series: The Rings of Power shows Harfoots as a nomadic folk who travel with the seasons.

places.note: The Stoor-kin Sméagol lived near the Gladden Fields.
Stoors lived in the Angle between two rivers.
The three kinds mixed in the Shire.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Prologue, 'Concerning Hobbits'
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B (The Third Age)
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 2

title: Dúnedain: Descent, Long Life and the Rangers
blurb: The Dúnedain descend from the Men of Númenor. They lived long, kept lore, and served as kings, stewards and Rangers.
book:
The Dúnedain are the descendants of the Edain, the Men who helped the Elves against Morgoth and were rewarded with the island of Númenor. After its Downfall in S.A. 3319, Elendil and his sons came to Middle-earth and founded Arnor and Gondor.

The Dúnedain lived much longer than other Men, but the gift faded in later generations. Aragorn, who is of the line of Isildur, lived to be 210 in the Fourth Age. They also became fewer and mixed with lesser Men, and their wisdom declined in Gondor.

In the Third Age, the Rangers of the North kept watch in Eriador. They were the remnant of Arnor, hidden from most Hobbits and Men, and they guarded the Shire without being known. Their lords were the Chieftains, from Aranarth to Aragorn.

In the south, the Rangers of Ithilien held Gondor's land east of the Anduin. Faramir led them and was known as their captain. They hid in the woods and ambushed servants of Mordor from places such as Henneth Annûn.

Dúnedain of both kingdoms spoke Westron but valued Elvish. They were proud and watchful.

facts.Origin: Númenor; Elendil came to Middle-earth after the Downfall in S.A. 3319

places.note: Arnor was the northern kingdom founded by Elendil.
Gondor was the southern kingdom of the Dúnedain.
The Rangers of Ithilien use this hidden refuge.
Faramir's Rangers hold Ithilien against Mordor.

sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A
The Two Towers, Book IV, chapters 4 to 6

title: The Government of Gondor
blurb: Gondor was ruled by kings of Anárion's line and then by Ruling Stewards. Beacons warned of war, and the Tower Guard watched the Citadel.
book:
Gondor was founded in S.A. 3320 by Elendil's sons Isildur and Anárion. Kings of Anárion's line ruled it, first from Osgiliath and from T.A. 1640 from Minas Anor. The line failed in T.A. 2050, when Eärnur rode to Minas Morgul and did not return.

After that the Stewards ruled in the name of the king. The first Ruling Steward was Mardil Voronwë. The Stewards were of the House of Húrin, and the office usually passed from father to son. They held the white rod of office. They never sat on the throne but ruled from a plain black chair below it, in the name of the king until he should return. Their banner was plain white.

The realm was divided into fiefs. Great lords governed them, such as the Prince of Dol Amroth, the lords of Lamedon and Lossarnach, and the lord of Pinnath Gelin. Each owed service to the Steward.

Beacons stood on hills along the White Mountains. The lighting of one signalled war. Seven are named: Amon Dîn, Eilenach, Nardol, Erelas, Min-Rimmon, Calenhad and Halifirien. The chain carried the call from Minas Tirith west toward Rohan.

The Guards of the Citadel wore black, marked with a white tree beneath a silver crown and stars. Some kept watch by the White Tree in the Court of the Fountain. Beregond was one of them.
film: In the film, Pippin lights the first beacon in Minas Tirith, and the beacons are shown being lit as a chain.

places.note: The Kings and later the Stewards ruled Gondor from this city.
Amon Dîn is the first beacon seen from Minas Tirith.
Min-Rimmon is a beacon on the road to Rohan.
Halifirien is the last beacon before Rohan.
Calenhad carries the beacon-call westward.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion)
The Return of the King, Book V, chapters 1 and 4

title: The Customs and Army of Rohan
kind: Riders and traditions of the Mark
blurb: The Rohirrim fight as horsemen in companies called éoreds, under Marshals of the Mark. They bury their kings in grassy mounds.
book:
The army of Rohan was a force of mounted spearmen and archers. Its basic unit was the éored, a company of riders who served under a captain. In war they rode with the king and his captains.

The king commanded his Riders through marshals. Éomer and Elfhelm held the title Marshal of the Mark. The Master of the Westfold, like Erkenbrand, led the men of the west.

The Rohirrim loved horses and ranked them with honour. Their finest were the Mearas, which would bear only the King of the Mark or his sons, until Shadowfax. Eorl's horse Felaróf was the first of them known to Men. Shadowfax, of the same breed, chose Gandalf as his rider.

The kings of the Mark were buried in mounds, in two lines beside the road below Edoras. The mounds were covered with simbelmynë, a white flower that bloomed all year. The people called it Evermind.

Riders who fell on the Pelennor were buried there in a mound. Théoden fell in that battle. His body lay first in Minas Tirith and was later carried home and laid in a mound at Edoras.

The kings held court in Meduseld, the golden hall of Edoras.

facts.Officers: Marshals of the Mark, Master of the Westfold

places.note: Edoras is the capital of Rohan.
Meduseld is the golden hall of the kings.
Barrowfield holds the burial mounds of the kings of the Mark.
The Mound of Riders on the Pelennor holds fallen Rohirrim.
Snowmane's Howe on the Pelennor holds Théoden's horse.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (The House of Eorl)
The Two Towers, Book III, chapters 2 and 6
The Return of the King, Book V, chapters 5 and 6; Book VI, chapter 6

title: The Dwarves: Houses, Secret Names and Durin's Day
blurb: Dwarves came from seven Fathers, hide their true names, keep Durin's Day as their New Year, and have few women.
book:
The Dwarves say that Aulë made seven Fathers, from whom seven Houses came. Durin's was the eldest, the Longbeards, who founded Khazad-dûm. The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion do not name the other six Houses. Names for them appear only in late notes by Tolkien published outside these books.

Every Dwarf has a secret true name, which he does not speak to outsiders. He is known by an outer name taken from the speech of Men. Even on a tomb the true name is not shown.

Durin's Day is the first day of the Dwarves' New Year. It falls when the last moon of autumn and the sun are in the sky together. Thrór's map said that the last light of the sun on Durin's Day would show the keyhole of the secret door of Erebor. On that evening Thorin's company found it.

Gimli said that dwarf-women are few, probably no more than a third of the people. They look and dress much like the men, and they seldom travel. Many dwarf-men never marry, so the race grows slowly. Dís, the sister of Thorin, is the only dwarf-woman named in these histories.

The books show Dwarves laid in tombs of stone. Balin lies in a stone tomb in Moria. Thorin is buried deep beneath the Mountain with the Arkenstone on his breast.

facts.Women: No more than a third of the people
facts.Durin's Day: First day of the Dwarves' year

places.note: The secret door of Erebor opened on Durin's Day.
The Longbeards of Durin founded this great realm.
Some of Durin's Folk later settled in the Iron Hills.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (Durin's Folk)
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F
The Hobbit, chapters 3, 11 and 18
The Silmarillion, chapter 2

title: The Faithful, the King's Men and the Black Númenóreans
blurb: Númenor divided into the Faithful, who honoured the Valar and Elves, and the King's Men, who defied them. Black Númenóreans served Sauron.
book:
In later Númenor the people split. The Faithful stayed friends of the Elves and honoured the Valar. They were a small group, living mostly in the west of the island until the kings moved many of them east. Elendil and his sons belonged to them.

The King's Men were the opposing party. They were proud, feared death, and resented the Ban of the Valar. They followed the kings who grew hostile to the Elves, and Ar-Pharazôn made them powerful. They oppressed the Faithful. At the urging of Sauron, Ar-Pharazôn had the White Tree Nimloth cut down and burned.

When Ar-Pharazôn led a fleet against Valinor, Númenor was drowned. The Faithful who had prepared ships escaped to Middle-earth. Some King's Men already held havens on the coasts, such as Umbar.

Some of these Númenóreans in Middle-earth became the Black Númenóreans. They served Sauron and hated the Faithful. Their lords held Umbar against Gondor until Gondor took it in T.A. 933. The Mouth of Sauron is described as one of their race.

Tolkien uses these names for the two sides of the old quarrel and for its heirs in Middle-earth.
series: The Rings of Power shows Númenor divided between those who welcome the Elves and those who distrust them.

places.note: Pelargir was a haven built by the Faithful on the Anduin.

sources: The Silmarillion, Akallabêth
The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A
The Return of the King, Book V, chapter 10

title: Wainriders, Balchoth and Variags
blurb: Eastern tribes pressed on Gondor for centuries. The Wainriders, the Balchoth and the Variags of Khand were named foes.
book:
The Easterlings came out of Rhûn in waves. The Wainriders began to attack Gondor in T.A. 1851. They were a league of tribes who travelled in great wains. In T.A. 1856 King Narmacil II fell in battle, Gondor lost its eastern lands, and the Northmen of Rhovanion were overrun.

The Wainriders attacked again in T.A. 1944. King Ondoher and his sons died in the fighting. Eärnil, captain of the Southern Army, then overthrew the enemy in their camp and drove the survivors into the Dead Marshes. He became king as Eärnil II.

The Balchoth were another Easterling people, wild and numerous. In T.A. 2510 they crossed the Anduin in boats and on rafts and drove the army of Gondor back onto the Field of Celebrant. Eorl and the Riders of the Éothéod came at Cirion's call and won the battle. Cirion then gave them Calenardhon, which became Rohan.

The Variags of Khand were Men of Khand, a land south-east of Mordor. They fought as allies of Mordor in the War of the Ring. At the Pelennor they appear with Southrons and Easterlings.

The books say little about their gods, tongues or homes.

places.note: Eärnil drove the Wainriders into the Dead Marshes.
The Field of Celebrant was the site of the Balchoth's defeat.
The Easterlings came out of the lands of Rhûn.
Easterlings and Variags marched with Sauron's host here.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion)
The Return of the King, Book V, chapters 4 and 6

title: The Haradrim and the Mûmakil
blurb: The Haradrim are the southern Men who fought for Sauron. They brought the mûmakil, huge war-beasts, to the Pelennor Fields.
book:
The Haradrim are the Men of Harad, in the south of Middle-earth. Gondor called them Southrons and often fought them. Near Harad lies close to Gondor's southern border. Far Harad is a remote land.

Most Haradrim served Sauron in the War of the Ring. In Ithilien, Faramir's Rangers ambush a column of Southrons on the road to Mordor. Sam sees a dead Southron and wonders about his life and home.

The mûmakil, which Sam calls oliphaunts, are huge beasts of Harad. Each carries a tower of fighters on its back. Their size and strength shake any line of battle. Sam knows a rhyme about them, and then he sees one.

At the Pelennor Fields the mûmakil advance with the army of Mordor. Horses fear them, and the Rohirrim cannot easily charge them. In the end the mûmakil are slain or driven off. The chieftain of the Haradrim rides under a black serpent on scarlet. Théoden kills him.

The books give few details about Haradrim customs, gods or cities. Tolkien leaves most of the far South untold.
film: In the films the mûmakil are huge elephant-like beasts, and Legolas climbs one and brings it down with his arrows.

places.note: The Haradrim come from the lands south of Gondor.
The mûmakil fight here on the side of Mordor.
Faramir's men ambush Southrons in South Ithilien.

sources: The Two Towers, Book IV, chapters 3 and 4
The Return of the King, Book V, chapters 4 and 6

title: The Corsairs of Umbar
blurb: The Corsairs of Umbar descended from the rebels of the Kin-strife. They raided Gondor's coasts for centuries and joined Sauron's war.
book:
Umbar was a Númenórean haven in the south. In T.A. 1432 a civil war began in Gondor, called the Kin-strife. Castamir the Usurper seized the throne in 1437 and was killed in 1447. In 1448 his sons and followers fled with many ships and seized Umbar. Their descendants became the Corsairs of Umbar.

The Corsairs built a fleet and raided the coasts of Gondor for centuries. They often joined the Southrons. Telumehtar Umbardacil took Umbar in T.A. 1810 and drove out the Corsairs. Gondor later lost it again, and the Corsairs went on raiding its coasts. Late in the Third Age Thorongil, who was Aragorn in disguise, burned many of their ships at Umbar.

During the War of the Ring, the Corsairs sailed north toward Pelargir. Sauron meant to use them against Gondor from the south. Aragorn fell on them at Pelargir on 13 March in T.A. 3019 and took their ships. Aragorn's men and recruits from the southern fiefs manned the captured ships. The fleet reached the Harlond on the Pelennor on 15 March.

places.note: Pelargir was the target of the Corsairs in T.A. 3019.
Aragorn defeated the Corsair fleet and took their ships.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion)
The Return of the King, Book V, chapters 1 and 9

title: The Northmen and the Éothéod
blurb: The Northmen were Men of Rhovanion who were friends of Gondor. From them came the Éothéod and later the Rohirrim.
book:
The Northmen lived in Rhovanion, the lands east and north of the Anduin. They were kin to the Edain of old and good friends of Gondor. Their king Vidugavia was a valued ally.

The friendship brought a great change to Gondor. Prince Valacar, who lived among the Northmen, married Vidugavia's daughter Vidumavi. Their son Eldacar was half-Northman. Some Gondorians disliked this, and it helped cause the Kin-strife that began in T.A. 1432.

The Northmen later suffered badly. The Wainriders overran them in T.A. 1856, and many were enslaved or driven away. Some of their kin survived in the vales of Anduin between the Carrock and the Gladden Fields.

Among them were the Éothéod, a people of horse-breeders. In T.A. 1977 Frumgar led them north. Their later lands lay near the sources of the Anduin, below the Grey Mountains. In T.A. 2510 their lord Eorl led riders south to help Gondor at the Field of Celebrant. As a reward, Cirion gave them Calenardhon, which became Rohan.

The Men of Dale, the Beornings and others belonged to the same northern family. The Rohirrim kept the old tongue and customs of the Northmen.

places.note: The Northmen lived in the lands called Rhovanion.
The Éothéod lived near the sources of the Anduin.
The Éothéod came to the Field of Celebrant in T.A. 2510.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A (Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion; The House of Eorl)
Unfinished Tales, 'Cirion and Eorl'

title: The Wise
kind: Elves, wizards and the White Council
blurb: In the books the Wise are those with lore and power. They include Elrond, Galadriel, Círdan, Gandalf and Saruman.
book:
The Wise is a loose name. The books use it for those who know the ancient lore and the secrets of the Enemy. They are mostly Elves and wizards, along with a few Men.

In T.A. 2463 the White Council was formed. Its members were Elrond, Galadriel, Círdan, Gandalf and Saruman, among others. The Council was formed soon after Sauron returned to Dol Guldur with greater strength. It met to decide how to respond.

Saruman was chosen as its head. He had studied the Rings more than any other. Galadriel had wished Gandalf to lead. In T.A. 2851 Gandalf urged an attack on Dol Guldur, but Saruman overruled him. The Council finally attacked in T.A. 2941 and drove Sauron out.

Gandalf and Saruman are the best-known members. Saruman ended as a traitor. His fall shows that wisdom is no guard against pride.

Other members acted differently. Elrond kept Rivendell, and Galadriel kept Lothlórien. Círdan guarded the Havens.

At the Council of Elrond, those present decided the fate of the Ring. The Wise did not rule the world. They advised and resisted in their own places.

places.note: Elrond held the Council of the Ring here.
Galadriel ruled this wood with Celeborn.
Dol Guldur was the target of the White Council in T.A. 2941.
Saruman later made Orthanc his stronghold.

sources: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B (The Third Age)
The Fellowship of the Ring, Book II, chapter 2

title: Emblems and Banners
blurb: Many peoples have emblems. The heirs of Elendil bear the White Tree, Rohan the White Horse, Mordor the Red Eye, Isengard the White Hand and Dol Amroth the swan-ship.
book:
The Stewards of Gondor flew a plain white banner. Aragorn came to the Pelennor under the royal standard, made by Arwen. It shows a white tree on black, with seven stars and a high crown, the signs of Elendil. The White Tree recalls Nimloth and the line of trees from it.

Rohan's banner shows a white horse running free on a green field. Théoden's host rode under it to the Pelennor.

Mordor uses a red Eye. Sauron's servants bore it on their shields and helms. It is also the symbol that Frodo and others dread.

Isengard uses a white hand on a black field. The Uruk-hai of Saruman wore a white hand on their helms and shields. The orcs of Minas Morgul carried another sign, a moon with a death-like face.

Dol Amroth has a ship like a silver swan, set on blue. The knights of Prince Imrahil rode under it, and the ship is part of the haven's long link with the sea and the Elves.

The Guards of the Citadel wore black, marked with a white tree beneath a silver crown and stars, like the royal sign.

Each emblem is tied to a place or a lord.
film: The films show the White Tree on Gondor's banners, the white horse on green for Rohan, and a white hand on Saruman's Uruk-hai.

facts.Gondor (royal): White Tree, seven stars, crown on black

places.note: The White Tree grows in the Court of the Fountain here.
Dol Amroth is the seat of the swan-ship banner.
Edoras is the seat of the White Horse.
Isengard bears the White Hand.
Barad-dûr bears the Red Eye.

title: Songs and Verse in the Books
aka: Poems in The Lord of the Rings
blurb: The books are full of songs. Hobbits sing walking and drinking songs, Elves sing hymns and laments, and Men of Rohan recall old kings.
book:
Songs and poems appear in many chapters. Tolkien uses them to show a speaker's character and a people's history.

Hobbits sing walking songs, bath songs, drinking songs and nonsense rhymes. Bilbo composed a famous road song. Frodo and his friends sing in the inns and on the road. Sam makes up a verse about trolls, and later sings in the tower of Cirith Ungol.

Elves sing hymns to the stars and laments for lost lands. Galadriel's farewell to Lothlórien is in Quenya. In Rivendell, Bilbo recites a long song about Eärendil. Legolas sings a song of Nimrodel.

The Dwarves sing slow songs of mountains and gold, as at Bag End. Gimli recites old verse about Durin. The goblins sing harsh songs in Goblin-town. Gollum makes riddles in verse.

Rohan has alliterative songs and laments. On the way to Edoras, Aragorn chants an old song of the Rohirrim about lost glory. Riders sing at the burial of Théoden.

Gandalf's charms and Tom Bombadil's verses are spells as well as songs.

Near Weathertop, Sam recites lines about Gil-galad, and Aragorn chants part of the tale of Beren and Lúthien.

places.note: Bilbo sings of Eärendil in Elrond's hall.
Galadriel's farewell lament is sung in Lothlórien.
Aragorn chants a song of the Rohirrim as the company nears Edoras.
Sam sings in the Tower of Cirith Ungol.

title: Food and Drink in the Books
blurb: Food runs through the story: travelling bread such as cram, the Ents' drink, Beorn's honey, wine and the Hobbits' home meals.
book:
Tolkien uses food to show character and place. Hobbits love stew, bacon, mushrooms, cakes, beer and tea. Sam is the cook of the Quest. He stews rabbit with herbs in Ithilien and carries pots and salt in his pack.

Cram is a hard, plain biscuit made for journeys. When the Elves give the Fellowship lembas, Gimli first takes it for cram and soon finds it far better.

In Fangorn, Treebeard gives Merry and Pippin Ent-draughts from great stone jars at Wellinghall. Later both Hobbits grow taller than any other Hobbit in the Shire records.

The Orcs force the captured Hobbits to drink a fiery orc-draught. It burns but gives them some strength.

Beorn feeds the Dwarves and Bilbo with bread, honey, cream and mead. He keeps bees, and he sends them off with twice-baked cakes for the road.

Wine is served in the halls of Men and Elves. Bilbo leaves Rory Brandybuck a dozen bottles of Old Winyards, a strong red wine of the Southfarthing. In The Hobbit, the Elvenking's butler and chief guard fall asleep over strong wine of Dorwinion, which lets Bilbo free the Dwarves.

Good drink and good food mark friendship in the story.

Lembas, miruvor and athelas have their own cards.

title: The Riddle-Game
blurb: The riddle-game is an ancient contest of riddles. Bilbo and Gollum play it under old rules that even wicked creatures fear to break.
book:
In the riddle-game two players ask riddles in turn. The one who fails to answer loses. The stakes are agreed at the start. Bilbo and Gollum play for their lives and their freedom.

Gollum proposes the game in the dark under the Misty Mountains. If Bilbo loses, Gollum will eat him. If Gollum loses, he will show Bilbo the way out. The narrator calls the game sacred and very old. Even wicked creatures fear to cheat in it.

The players trade riddles about teeth, the dark, time and other things. Bilbo wins some by luck and by quick thought. The last riddle is not a true one. Bilbo asks what he has in his pocket, which is the Ring.

Gollum protests that this is not fair and demands three guesses. Bilbo agrees. Gollum fails all three. He then goes to fetch the Ring so he can attack Bilbo, but finds it gone. Bilbo slips it on by chance and escapes.

Bilbo uses riddling speech again with Smaug. He gives answers that tell the dragon little and flatter him.

The meeting brings the Ring out of Gollum's keeping and into the Shire.

facts.Stakes: Bilbo's life against a way out

places.note: Gollum's Lake is the place where the contest was played.
The Misty Mountains hide the tunnels where they met.

title: Travel and Distance
kind: Journey times in the War of the Ring
blurb: This entry gives dates and days for the main journeys of the War of the Ring, from the Tale of Years.
book:
The books record dates carefully. Appendix B gives the days of the main journeys in T.A. 3018 and 3019. Its dates follow the Shire calendar. Every month has thirty days, and two Yule days fall between December and January.

Frodo left Bag End on 23 September 3018. He reached Bree on 29 September. He crossed the Ford of Bruinen on 20 October. From Bag End to the Ford took 27 days.

The Fellowship left Rivendell on 25 December. They came to the West-gate of Moria on 13 January and crossed the Bridge of Khazad-dûm on 15 January, when Gandalf fell. They reached the Nimrodel that night and left Lothlórien on 16 February. They camped at Parth Galen on 25 February, and the Fellowship broke on 26 February. From Rivendell to the breaking took 63 days, counting the two Yule days.

Frodo and Sam left Parth Galen on 26 February and reached the Cracks of Doom on 25 March. That is 29 days.

The Rohirrim rode from Harrowdale on 10 March and came to the Pelennor on 15 March, five days later. Aragorn took the ships at Pelargir on 13 March and reached the Pelennor on 15 March.

The four Hobbits left Rivendell with Gandalf on 5 October 3019 on their way home. The Battle of Bywater took place on 3 November, 28 days later.

Bilbo's earlier journey began in T.A. 2941, and he came home in 2942.
